sceneHappening: Pray for us, the Lord is faithful, and a firm word about idleness: if anyone will not work, he should not eat
summary: Finally, Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray for him and his friends "that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly and be glorified, even as also with you, and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil men; for not all have faith. But the Lord is faithful, who will establish you, and guard you from the evil one." Paul has confidence in the Lord that they both do and will do the things he commands, and he prays that the Lord would direct their hearts into the love of God and into the perseverance of Christ. "Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks in idleness and not after the tradition which they received from us." They know how they ought to imitate Paul and his friends, because they did not behave in idleness among them, nor did they eat bread from anyone without paying; "but in labor and travail worked night and day, that we might not burden any of you; not because we don't have the right, but to make ourselves an example to you, that you should imitate us." And when they were with them, they commanded this: "If any man will not work, neither let him eat." For they hear that some walk among them in idleness, "who don't work at all, but are busybodies. Now those who are such we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread." But they, brothers, are not to be weary in doing well. If anyone doesn't obey the word by this letter, "note that man, that you have no company with him, to the end that he may be ashamed. Don't count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother." Now may the Lord of peace himself give them peace at all times in all ways; the Lord be with them all. Paul writes the greeting with his own hand, "which is the sign in every letter. This is how I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen."
whySettingMatters: The command about work is a response to a practical problem rather than a general rule against helping the poor. Some Thessalonians seem to have stopped working, perhaps because they expected the Lord to return soon (the same concern as in 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12 and 5:14), and had begun to depend on others' generosity and to interfere in other people's affairs. Paul's answer is to point to his own example: he worked as a tentmaker so as not to be a burden, though as an apostle he had the right to support (1 Corinthians 9:3-18). The sentence "if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat" refers to those who "will not" work, not those who cannot; it has often been taken out of context. The advice to "note that man" and "have no company with him" is meant to produce shame and restoration, not rejection: "Don't count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother." The final lines, about the greeting in his own hand "which is the sign in every letter," are a response to the forged-letter worry of 2:2. This is also the point where some scholars see Paul himself asserting authorship; others read it as part of a letter written in his name.

people.note: Asks for prayer and gives a firm word about work, signing with his own hand.
Told to keep doing good and to work.
The evil one, from whom the Lord will guard them.
The faithful Lord and Lord of peace.

questions: Paul asks for prayer that the word may "spread rapidly." What does that image suggest about what prayer is for?
"If anyone will not work, neither let him eat." How does the setting (people who could but would not) change how the verse reads?
He tells them to "admonish him as a brother," not treat him as an enemy. How do firmness and care go together here?
Paul points to his own example rather than just giving rules. Why is example often stronger than instruction?
